title: Zechariah 4:1–14
context: Zechariah 4:1–14 is the fifth night vision in the common count. The interpreting angel, “the angel who talked with me”, wakes the prophet, who sees a lampstand all of gold with a bowl and seven lamps, and two olive trees beside it (4:1–3). When the prophet asks what these are, the angel answers with the LORD’s word to Zerubbabel: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (4:6). In context the word concerns the rebuilding of the temple. The great mountain before Zerubbabel will become a plain, he will bring out the capstone with shouts of “Grace, grace, to it!”, and the hands that laid the foundation will finish the house (4:7–9); Ezra 6:15 records the house finished in the sixth year of Darius. Those who despise “the day of small things” (4:10) are answered with joy at the plumb line in Zerubbabel’s hand; compare Ezra 3:12 and Haggai 2:3 on disappointment at the modest new house. The seven, often linked with the seven lamps or with the seven eyes of 3:9, are explained as “the LORD’s eyes, which run back and forth through the whole earth” (4:10). The two olive trees, also described as two olive branches, are “the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth” (4:14). They are commonly read as Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, though some readers suggest the prophets Haggai and Zechariah or take the figures more broadly; the text does not name them. Revelation 11:4 calls the two witnesses “the two olive trees and the two lamp stands”, using the image in its own setting without settling its meaning here. Historic, symbolic, and future readings of the vision appear in both traditions. Shared ground: the work of the LORD’s Spirit in 4:6 is affirmed in both traditions. The notes on 4:6 take up how God’s enabling relates to human labor.

verses.text: The angel who talked with me came again and wakened me, as a man who is wakened out of his sleep.
verses.arminianNotes: The interpreting angel, the angel who talked with the prophet, comes again and wakes him as a man is wakened out of sleep. Arminian readers note the prophet’s need to be roused to receive the vision, and they see God patiently drawing his servant into understanding.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same image and read it as God’s initiative in revelation, since the prophet does not wake himself. Shared ground: both traditions see the vision as a gift given, not a discovery made, and read the waking as the start of a new vision.

verses.text: He said to me, “What do you see?” I said, “I have seen, and behold, a lamp stand all of gold, with its bowl on the top of it, and its seven lamps on it; there are seven pipes to each of the lamps which are on the top of it;
verses.arminianNotes: The angel asks what the prophet sees, and Zechariah describes a lampstand all of gold with a bowl on top, seven lamps, and pipes to each lamp. Arminian readers recall the tabernacle lampstand of Exodus 25 and see light kept burning in God’s house for his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same tabernacle background and the abundant supply pictured in the bowl and pipes. Readers in both traditions take the lampstand as the restored community or the temple, and later Christian readers often compare the lampstands of Revelation 1:20 in their own setting.

verses.text: and two olive trees by it, one on the right side of the bowl, and the other on the left side of it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Two olive trees stand by the lampstand, one on the right side of the bowl and the other on the left. Arminian readers often note that the trees supply oil without human hands, an image of provision that does not depend on the strength of a small and struggling community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same image as a picture of God’s unfailing supply to his people. Shared ground: both traditions see the trees as sources of oil for the lamp, and both hold their identity open until the angel explains them in 4:14.

verses.text: I answered and spoke to the angel who talked with me, saying, “What are these, my lord?”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet asks the angel who talked with him, “What are these, my lord?” Arminian readers see an example of honest inquiry, and they note that the visions in Zechariah regularly unfold through questions and answers between the prophet and the interpreting angel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same pattern and read it as a sign that the meaning of the vision comes from God rather than from the prophet’s own insight. Shared ground: both traditions value the prophet’s humility in asking and the angel’s readiness to answer him.

verses.text: Then the angel who talked with me answered me, “Don’t you know what these are?” I said, “No, my lord.”
verses.arminianNotes: The angel asks, “Don’t you know what these are?” and the prophet answers, “No, my lord.” Arminian readers hear a gentle prompting that invites the prophet to admit his need, and they note that understanding comes here through patient dialogue rather than sudden insight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same exchange as underlining that the vision cannot be understood apart from revelation given by God. Shared ground: both traditions read the prophet’s plain admission as fitting humility before a word that comes from the LORD and not from himself.

verses.text: Then he answered and spoke to me, saying, “This is the LORD’s word to Zerubbabel, saying, ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: The angel gives the LORD’s word to Zerubbabel: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit”. Arminian readers read the word in context as encouragement for the temple rebuilding, and they hear God’s Spirit enabling Zerubbabel and the people to do the work they were called to do.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same word as placing the completion of the temple wholly in God’s power, with the people’s labor as the means he uses. Shared ground: the Spirit’s work is affirmed in both traditions. On how God’s enabling relates to human labor, see the Psalms 127:1 box; compare Philippians 2:13 and 1 Corinthians 15:10.

verses.text: Who are you, great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you are a plain; and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of ‘Grace, grace, to it!’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The great mountain before Zerubbabel will become a plain, and he will bring out the capstone with shouts of “Grace, grace, to it!” Arminian readers read the mountain as the obstacles to rebuilding, such as the opposition recorded in Ezra 4–5, and they hear grace celebrated at the work’s completion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the same mountain and hear the shout of grace as the community confessing that the finished house is God’s gift. The capstone is read by some as the top stone and by others as a chief or foundation stone, and the sense remains uncertain in both traditions.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to the prophet, a formula that marks the next part of the message. Arminian readers note that the prophet passes on what he receives, and they read the shift from vision to spoken word as a reminder that the visions serve the LORD’s message to his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same formula and read it as the LORD’s authority standing behind what follows. Shared ground: both traditions see 4:8–10 as a word that interprets the vision for Zerubbabel and for the rebuilding community in Jerusalem.

verses.text: “The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house. His hands shall also finish it; and you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me to you.
verses.arminianNotes: The hands of Zerubbabel laid the foundation of this house, and his hands will finish it. Arminian readers note that Ezra 6:15 records the house finished in the sixth year of Darius, and they see the promise fulfilled through a leader who kept working.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same fulfillment and stress that the completion confirms the messenger: “you will know that the LORD of Armies has sent me to you.” Readers differ on who is sent here, the prophet or the angel of the LORD, and the identification is uncertain.

verses.text: Indeed, who despises the day of small things? For these seven shall rejoice, and shall see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel. These are the LORD’s eyes, which run back and forth through the whole earth.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD rebukes those who despise the day of small things, and the seven rejoice at the plumb line in Zerubbabel’s hand. Arminian readers recall the old men who wept at the modest new foundation in Ezra 3:12, and they hear encouragement for faithful work in small beginnings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse with Haggai 2:3 and stress that the LORD’s eyes, which run back and forth through the whole earth, see and govern the work. The seven are often linked with the lamps of 4:2 or the seven eyes of 3:9, though the link is debated.

verses.text: Then I asked him, “What are these two olive trees on the right side of the lamp stand and on the left side of it?”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet asks about the two olive trees on the right side and on the left side of the lampstand. Arminian readers note the prophet’s persistence in seeking the meaning, and they see the question drawing the vision toward the identity of those who serve beside the light.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same question and read the persistence as a mark of the prophet’s concern for the leadership of the restored community. Shared ground: both traditions read the trees as central to the vision and wait for the angel’s answer in 4:14.

verses.text: I asked him the second time, “What are these two olive branches, which are beside the two golden spouts that pour the golden oil out of themselves?”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet asks a second time, now of two olive branches beside two golden spouts that pour out golden oil. Arminian readers see the oil flowing freely, an image of supply given to the lampstand, and they hear in the repeated question an earnest desire to understand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same flow and read the golden oil as a picture of God’s rich provision through his appointed servants. The details of the branches and spouts are difficult, and readers in both traditions hold their explanation loosely rather than pressing each part.

verses.text: He answered me, “Don’t you know what these are?” I said, “No, my lord.”
verses.arminianNotes: The angel again asks, “Don’t you know what these are?” and the prophet again answers, “No, my lord.” Arminian readers hear the repetition slowing the scene before the answer, and they note that the prophet does not pretend to knowledge he lacks.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same repetition as emphasizing that the identity of the two must be revealed rather than guessed. Shared ground: both traditions read the prophet’s second admission as humility that prepares for the angel’s explanation in the next verse.

verses.text: Then he said, “These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.”
verses.arminianNotes: The angel says, “These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth.” Arminian readers commonly take them as Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, though some suggest the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, and the text does not name them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hold the same common reading with the same caution, and they note that Revelation 11:4 uses olive trees and lampstands for two witnesses in its own setting, named here without harmonizing. Some Christian readers also see in the pairing of ruler and priest a hint of Christ, compare 6:12–13.
